title: Diversity & the protected characteristics
blurb: Name all nine protected characteristics of the Equality Act 2010 and spot when a project decision treats someone less favourably.
question: On a rail signalling upgrade, a project manager leaves a 61-year-old engineer off training for the new testing software, saying 'she'll be retiring soon, so it's not worth it'. Which protected characteristic is this decision based on, and why is it a problem?

teach.body: Diversity means recognising, respecting and valuing the differences between people: their backgrounds, experiences, identities and ways of thinking. Inclusion is what makes diversity work: making sure everyone can take part, is heard and feels valued. In plain English, diversity is the mix of people on your project; inclusion is making that mix work. UK law protects nine of those differences in particular: the protected characteristics of the Equality Act 2010.

teach.caption: They run in alphabetical order. Memory hook: 'All Dogs Get Muddy Paws Running Round Sandy Shores'.

teach.caption: Three names have two parts but count as ONE characteristic each: marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, religion or belief.

teach.body: Treating someone less favourably because of a protected characteristic is discrimination, and the Equality Act 2010 makes it unlawful. It covers recruitment, pay, training, promotion, task allocation and dismissal, and also how services are provided to customers. Project managers make people decisions every day (who joins, who leads, who gets the overtime or the training), so these rules apply directly to them, whatever the life cycle or sector.

rows.label: What it is
values: Worse treatment because of a characteristic
A rule for all that disadvantages a group

rows.label: Project example
values: Not promoting someone for their age

rows.label: Intent needed?
values: No: the reason is what counts
No: the effect is what counts
No: purpose or effect is enough

teach.caption: Indirect discrimination can be lawful only if the rule is objectively justified. Treating someone badly for raising a complaint is victimisation, also unlawful.

teach.h: Where it applies on a project

children.label: Suppliers' staff
children.sub: expect partners to treat people fairly

teach.text: The exam lists distractors that sound protected but are not: social class, education, length of service, job title, working pattern. And watch two real ones: NATIONALITY is protected (it is part of race), and AGE protects everyone, young as well as old. There are NINE characteristics, not ten or twelve.

teach.body: Leanne, the project manager, builds a night-shift testing rota. She leaves Sam, who is pregnant, off it 'for her own good' without asking her, and skips training for Pat, 61, 'as she'll retire soon'. Both decisions are based on protected characteristics (pregnancy and maternity; age). The fair route: talk to Sam and use a proper risk assessment with the safety team, and offer Pat the training on the same basis as everyone else.

items.label: the Equality Act that lists them
Act that brought earlier separate equality laws together

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the relevant protected characteristic(s) precisely, using the Act's wording.
State that less favourable treatment because of it is discrimination and unlawful.
Explain the project decision affected (selection, tasks, training, promotion, service).
Say what a fair, objective basis for the decision would be (skills, evidence, agreed criteria).
Add the consequence of getting it wrong: harm to people, legal claims, reputation, lost talent.
Nine protected characteristics (Equality Act 2010): age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation.
Treating someone less favourably because of one is discrimination.
Race includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origin; age covers all ages.
Social class, education and length of service are NOT protected characteristics.
It applies to every people decision on a project and to how users are served.

summary: You can now name all nine protected characteristics of the Equality Act 2010 and explain what each covers. You can also recognise when a project decision treats someone less favourably because of one, and reject the look-alike distractors the exam uses.

A.q: Which of the following is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?
A.why: Gender reassignment is one of the nine protected characteristics. It protects people proposing to undergo, undergoing or who have undergone a process to reassign their sex.

whyNot.0: Social class (socio-economic background) is not one of the nine protected characteristics.
whyNot.1: Length of service is not a protected characteristic, although it must not be used as a cover for age discrimination.
whyNot.3: Educational background is not a protected characteristic.

A.q: How many protected characteristics does the Equality Act 2010 list?
A.why: There are nine: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.

whyNot.0: Seven is too few: it leaves out two of the nine characteristics.
whyNot.1: Ten is a common guess if 'pregnancy' and 'maternity' are counted separately; they form one characteristic.
whyNot.2: Twelve would only come from splitting the three two-part names; each counts as one.

A.q: A project manager leaves a 61-year-old engineer off training for new software, saying 'she'll retire soon, so it isn't worth it'. Which protected characteristic is this decision based on?
A.why: The decision is based on the engineer's age and an assumption about retirement. Denying training because of age is less favourable treatment because of a protected characteristic.

whyNot.1: Nothing in the scenario relates to an impairment.
whyNot.2: The reason given is retirement, which is linked to age, not to being a woman.
whyNot.3: Her relationship status plays no part in the decision.

B.q: Which is NOT one of the nine protected characteristics?
B.why: Socio-economic background is not a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010, even though many organisations choose to monitor it.

whyNot.0: Pregnancy and maternity is a protected characteristic (one characteristic, not two).
whyNot.2: Sexual orientation is a protected characteristic.
whyNot.3: Religion or belief, including having no belief, is a protected characteristic.

B.q: A subcontractor's site manager refuses to let a Polish electrician lead a work package because he 'prefers British supervisors'. Which statement is correct?
options: Nationality isn't covered by the Act
Only religion or belief is relevant
Race covers nationality, so it applies
It's lawful if the client agrees to it
B.why: Under the Equality Act 2010, race includes colour, nationality and ethnic or national origins. Treating the electrician less favourably because of his nationality is race discrimination.

whyNot.0: Nationality is covered: it is part of the race characteristic.
whyNot.1: Nothing in the scenario concerns religion; the reason given is nationality.
whyNot.3: A client cannot make discrimination lawful by agreeing to it.

B.q: A project insists that everyone works on site 7am to 7pm with no flexibility. The rule applies to all, but disadvantages many women with childcare duties. If it cannot be objectively justified, what could this be?
B.why: Indirect discrimination is a rule applied to everyone that puts people with a protected characteristic (here, sex) at a particular disadvantage and cannot be objectively justified.

whyNot.0: Direct discrimination is treating a person worse BECAUSE of their characteristic; this rule treats everyone the same on paper.
whyNot.1: Victimisation is treating someone badly for making or supporting a complaint.
whyNot.2: Harassment is unwanted conduct that violates dignity; this is a working-hours rule.

C.q:
Which THREE of the following are protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010?
1. Religion or belief
2. Trade union membership
3. Sexual orientation
4. Pregnancy and maternity
C.why: Religion or belief, sexual orientation, and pregnancy and maternity are all among the nine protected characteristics.

whyNot.0: Trade union membership (2) is protected by separate employment law, but it is not one of the nine Equality Act characteristics.
whyNot.2: Includes trade union membership (2), which is not an Equality Act characteristic.
whyNot.3: Includes trade union membership (2) and leaves out sexual orientation (3), which is protected.

C.q: At a team social, a colleague keeps making 'jokes' about a team member's religion, which leave her feeling humiliated. He says it was only banter. Which statement is correct?
options: It's fine as no formal decision was made
It may be harassment, whatever he meant
It's only unlawful if she complains in writing
It's acceptable if others found it funny
C.why: Harassment is unwanted conduct related to a protected characteristic that violates someone's dignity or creates a humiliating or offensive environment. Intent is not required: the effect on the person matters.

whyNot.0: Discrimination law is not limited to formal decisions; conduct and behaviour are covered too.
whyNot.2: Whether conduct is unlawful does not depend on how a complaint is made.
whyNot.3: Other people's amusement does not change the impact on the person targeted.

C.q: A project manager decides not to put a pregnant engineer on the night-shift rota 'to protect her', without asking her. What should the project manager have done instead?
options: Moved her to part-time hours until her leave
Asked HR to bring forward her maternity leave
Talked with her and assessed the actual risks
Kept the decision quiet to avoid upsetting her
C.why: Decisions about a pregnant worker should be based on a real risk assessment and a conversation with her, not on assumptions. Removing her from work without that is less favourable treatment because of pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Changing her hours without discussion is another assumption-based decision.
whyNot.1: The project manager should not try to change her leave; that is her choice within her rights.
whyNot.3: Secrecy doesn't make an unfair decision fair, and it removes her chance to have a say.

reteach.title: Picking who works the busy Saturday shift
reteach.question: Imagine you manage a busy restaurant and must choose who works the big Saturday service. Which reasons are fair to use, and which nine must never be the reason?

blocks.body: You can fairly choose staff on skill, experience, availability and past performance. What you must never base the choice on is who they are: their age, a disability, gender reassignment, being married or in a civil partnership, being pregnant or on maternity leave, their race, religion or belief, sex or sexual orientation. A project team works the same way: decide on the work, never on those nine.

blocks.caption: Swap 'Saturday shift' for 'lead the design workstream' and the rule is identical on a project.

blocks.text: Keep the nine to nine: two-part names (marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, religion or belief) each count once.

explain.body: Diversity is the mix: the differences between people in background, identity, experience and thinking. Inclusion is making the mix work, so everyone can take part, is heard and feels valued. You can have a diverse team that isn't inclusive, and then the benefits are lost.

test.q: Which statement best describes the difference between diversity and inclusion?
options: Diversity is the mix; inclusion lets all take part
Diversity is a legal duty; inclusion is optional
Diversity means quotas; inclusion means training
They mean exactly the same thing in practice
test.why: Diversity describes the mix of different people; inclusion is the practice of making sure all of them can participate and feel valued.

whyNot.1: The legal duty is not to discriminate; inclusion is the good practice that makes diversity work, not an optional extra.
whyNot.2: Diversity is not the same as quotas, and inclusion is much broader than training.
whyNot.3: They are related but different: a team can be diverse without being inclusive.

explain.body: Age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation. Gender reassignment protects anyone proposing to undergo, undergoing or who has undergone a process to reassign their sex.

items.label: have two-part names but count once

test.q: Which protected characteristic covers someone who is proposing to undergo, is undergoing, or has undergone a process to reassign their sex?
test.why: This is the definition of the gender reassignment characteristic.

whyNot.0: Sex refers to being a man or a woman.
whyNot.1: Sexual orientation is about who a person is attracted to.
whyNot.2: Marriage and civil partnership concerns being married or a civil partner.

explain.body: Direct discrimination is treating someone worse because of a protected characteristic. Indirect discrimination is a rule applied to everyone that disadvantages a protected group without objective justification. Motive doesn't matter: the reason and the effect do.

rows.label: Problem
values: The effect falls on a group

test.q: A team member is passed over for a lead role shortly after telling her manager about her same-sex partner, although she was the strongest candidate. If the reason was her sexual orientation, what is this?
test.why: Treating someone less favourably because of their sexual orientation is direct discrimination.

whyNot.0: Indirect discrimination involves a general rule that disadvantages a group; here one person was treated worse because of who she is.
whyNot.2: A decision based on a protected characteristic is not a fair business decision.
whyNot.3: Positive action is lawful steps to help under-represented groups; this is the opposite.

explain.body: The characteristics apply whenever you decide about people: recruiting, allocating tasks and overtime, choosing who gets training or promotion, and serving customers. Project managers make these decisions constantly, so they must base them on objective, job-related reasons.

test.q:
Which of these project decisions must be free of discrimination because of a protected characteristic?
1. Recruiting a team member
2. Allocating paid overtime
3. Choosing who attends training
4. Serving customers of a public service
test.why: All four are covered: the Equality Act applies to recruitment, the terms and opportunities of work (overtime, training) and the provision of services to the public.

whyNot.0: Overtime (2) and customer service (4) are covered too.
whyNot.1: Serving customers of a public service (4) is also covered.
whyNot.2: Equality law goes well beyond recruitment.
